Text | Fanyu Meng

Editing | Er Mu, Fanyu Meng

Facebook Reality Labs (FRL) either grew out of Oculus, or Oculus moved into FRL after it was acquired; I’m not entirely sure which. This isn’t a history article, though, so I’ll be lazy for once and let keen readers Google it (or Baidu it) themselves. Oculus was the VR headset company that rode highest on the VR wave of a few years ago. A little over a month after Facebook bought WhatsApp, Oculus became the next “chosen child” and was snapped up by FB too. Today I want to talk about FRL’s audio team.

Not long ago FRL’s audio team put out a set of seriously cool press stories. I love them, and I think the team really is at the cutting edge of acoustics: their research is interesting and has real potential. So this article is built around their news and research directions, to show how acoustics and audio are done at Facebook. At the end I’ll open the floor; all views are welcome.

If you know anyone at FRL, please pass on the message that a Chinese guy is doing their PR for free, and that a little gratitude would be appreciated.

The head of FRL’s audio team is Ravish Mehra, from India: he’s the one pondering the meaning of life below. He graduated from the University of North Carolina in 2014 and is already leading a team at a young age. Hats off.

Cue the voice of Michael Jordan, also a UNC man: “Ah, my young fellow alum! How I miss our days learning to drive excavators at school.” (Excavator school being the classic Chinese meme for vocational training.)

Then another voice: “Do American tech companies all like Indian bosses?”

The news released on September 3 set out FRL’s main areas of acoustics research. They range widely, across 3D audio, audio for AR glasses, hearing aids, AI, speech recognition, music and more. Let’s look at what they are actually doing.

FRL’s audio research falls into two broad categories:

  • Creating virtual sounds that are indistinguishable from real ones

  • Redefining human hearing and creating perceptual superpowers

As the ancient proverb goes: exciting!

1. 3D audio

The kindly bearded gentleman below is one of the main developers of FRL’s 3D audio. He has a long connection with Dr. Song Li from our team of science writers: they have worked together before and are now colleagues at Facebook.

Research scientist Pablo Hoffmann

1 HRTF

The video below shows the basic principles of 3D audio and some of the knowledge behind it, such as the interaural level difference (ILD), room reflections and HRTFs. With its slick visual effects, it makes jargon that might otherwise sound like black magic very intuitive. I have touched on these topics more or less in earlier articles:

A history of acoustics: psychoacoustics, part 1

A history of acoustics: architectural acoustics

Truly realistic 3D audio: you can’t tell virtual from real

HRTFs are normally measured in an anechoic chamber. The subject sits inside with microphones in their ears, while an arc of loudspeakers plays a test signal, such as a sine sweep. The measured transfer function captures the effect of the upper torso, head and ears on the sound. Rotate the loudspeaker arc through 360 degrees and you have a full-sphere HRTF dataset for that person, with a spatial resolution set by the number of loudspeakers. The video says HRTFs can be predicted from a photo of the ear. It’s a very sexy idea, and I’m curious how accurate it can get.

Let me plug a recent review on HRTFs by Dr. Song Li:

Measurement of Head-Related Transfer Functions: A Review

And while I’m at it, a nudge to him: once the noise-cancelling series is done, how about writing about HRTFs too?

Everything you wanted to know about noise-cancelling headphones, part 1

Everything you wanted to know about noise-cancelling headphones, part 2: adaptive feedforward ANC

The next two videos let you hear a virtual moving source and a virtual source with physical size. Headphones on, please.

3D audio: a virtual moving source

3D audio: a virtual source with volume

Apple is investing heavily in this area too, and in China so is Huawei; they are all looking at and solving the same problems. It’s good that the giants are all at it. It keeps acoustics moving forward and keeps food on the table for those of us in the field.

2 Virtual rooms

Here FRL mainly talks about video conferencing: giving you the feeling of being in the room even when you’re not. For example, the position where you see each person can be matched to the direction their voice comes from, as if you were really sitting in the meeting. Personally this doesn’t excite me much. All the online meetings since the pandemic began have given me enough headaches already, and I don’t think 3D audio would make me feel any better about them, however real the sights and sounds. Or rather, none of the 3D audio I have heard has been all that realistic, so my enthusiasm for this use is limited. But that is exactly what those of us in the field need to solve, and prove.

2. What you see is what you hear

Wearing AR glasses could enhance your hearing, so you can follow what people say even in noisy surroundings. That is genuinely meaningful. A few decades from now, I won’t hesitate to buy a dozen pairs.

The video below mentions several key technologies: beamforming, machine learning and active noise control. AR glasses will carry lots of microphones and use beamforming to scan for sources, like radar. If there are many prominent sources, which one should you listen to? Sensors on the glasses track your head and eye movements to work out which sound you are interested in; machine learning will certainly come in here. Active noise control, I would guess, comes in once the main source has been identified, to cancel the other interfering sources. Beamforming does the same job, of course, so using both is a double attack that works better. Ideally, as the video shows, you can hear the person across from you in a bar without having to go cheek to cheek.

Hearing enhancement in noisy environments

Wang Jianguo, forced to talk cheek to cheek with Hu Lan in a nightclub (both are Chinese stand-up comedians)

Another practical technology is near-field beamforming, which lets the microphone focus on the sound from your mouth during a phone call while suppressing background noise from other directions. This inevitably needs the what-you-see-is-what-you-hear technology above, plus a monitoring function so that at the very least you can hear yourself speak. Otherwise, when the background noise is loud and your own voice is quiet, you won’t even know what you’re saying…

Near-field beamforming: no more shouting into the phone

3. Human hearing

The medical device industry may want to start worrying: the tech giants are gradually moving into hearing and hearing aids.

This reminds me of an episode of the British TV drama Casualty that I watched a while ago. It is about a girl born with hearing loss, who was abandoned by her mother as a child because of it. The clip below shows her meeting her birth mother for the first time. It also portrays the daily life of people with hearing impairment and what the world sounds like to them.

Hearing aids still have a lot of room for improvement. How to improve the listening experience of people with hearing loss remains a hard problem, but a deeply meaningful one.

What does sound through a hearing aid sound like?

And here I have to give a shout-out to my senior labmate far away in North America: we’re waiting for your article! I know too little to say much here, so look forward to her masterpiece :)

FRL is now developing in-ear monitors (IEMs) that handle active noise control. Removing unwanted background noise lets you hear the sounds you want more clearly and safely. The IEMs also have a hear-through function: with the device in, you can still hear the outside world as if you weren’t wearing anything.

In the United States, one in five people struggles with hearing loss. For all sorts of reasons, including cost, comfort and trust, many of them don’t wear hearing aids. Beyond AR glasses, FRL is also working on hearing science and trying to move the field forward.

4. Privacy

Westerners generally care more about personal privacy, though I think there’s no need to be quite so nervous. A colleague of mine once uninstalled WhatsApp after Facebook bought it, saying he was worried Zuckerberg would get hold of his private data. I was lost for words and could only salute him as a true hero.

FRL says there need to be rules for people who use AR glasses. For example, a user’s voice may be amplified only with that user’s consent. Other personal information, such as data about a person’s ears, must also be protected: available only to researchers and never made public.

5. The frontier: machine perception of sound

One of FRL’s main goals is to develop high-tech AR glasses that provide not only visual but also auditory information, letting users interact with the world around them. The glasses scan the world around you and present the information you want. Walk into a restaurant, for example, and the AR glasses can recognize what is going on around you: people talking, the air conditioning humming, plates and glasses clinking. Using AI, the glasses can automatically identify and remove interfering noise.

Facebook LiveMaps: the AR world of the future

Another cool feature is breaking down language barriers: speech recognition and AI can automatically translate what someone says to you in a foreign language.

To sum up, in the words of the head of FRL’s audio team:

“Five or 10 years from now, if somebody joins the field, they’ll be chasing tail lights. At this moment, we can actually define what the future can be. We can make things so real that you don’t need to travel hundreds or thousands of miles to attend a meeting or connect with your loved ones. We can build technologies that can be used to improve human hearing.”

I’ll leave this article open-ended too. Rather than sum up, I’ll hand the floor to you: what do you think of Facebook’s acoustics research, and where are acoustics and audio heading?
